```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 110,
  warning = FALSE, message = FALSE
)
```

Every plot family the package has, drawn on two real CEF data sets, to look
at and to check that each draws sensibly: discard, length and age coverage,
discard rate, and length and age distributions - each with a few options to
compare against each other. It is ggplot2 only: every plot function returns
a ggplot object (or `NULL` when there is nothing to draw).

This is the first of four vignettes. Once the data has been explored here,
**2a** and **2b** define groups of strata and raise the discards - by hand
and with the hierarchical cascade - and **3** compares group allocation
schemes.

This is a walkthrough, not a test: nothing here asserts pass or fail. It is
also the script to run chunk by chunk in RStudio; every figure is simply
printed.

**Table first.** The coverage and discard-rate figures are drawn from the
table `build_coverage_strata()` returns, and every one of them takes either
the raw catch (the table is built for you, at exactly the plotted columns) or
that table itself. Section 2 first shows the tables on their own - discard
rates and coverage per stratum, at whatever aggregation you name - and then
the same numbers as figures.

**Length plots stay on the landings.** Nothing in this vignette ever raises
or allocates: it only has raw catch. A length plot on `catchCategory = "Dis"`
would show the discards' *own*, un-raised length sample as if it were the
whole picture - a coverage plot would look fully sampled when it is not, and
a distribution plot would show a shape that has not been weighted up to what
was actually discarded. So length and age views use `"Lan"` throughout.

**Nothing is filtered first.** The app lets you narrow a figure to a subset
(a country, a year, an area); here every plot uses everything in the loaded
table. To plot a subset, filter the catch or the distributions yourself
before the call - every function takes a plain data frame.

# Data

Two stocks, read from the CEF csv files under `inst/extdata/data_CEF_format`
(local to this machine; the files are not in the repository).

* **brill**, `bll.27.3a47de`, 2025 - discards and lengths. It has no age
  data, so an age plot on it would draw an empty or misleading panel rather
  than erroring.
* **saithe**, `pok.27.3a46`, 2022 - the one with ages, and no length data.

```{r load}
library(dplyr)
library(rcef)

cef_dir <- file.path("..", "inst", "extdata", "data_CEF_format")

# blank cells (no discard domain, no trip count ...) read as NA
catch_data        <- read.csv(file.path(cef_dir, "bll", "bll_2025_catches_CEF_v17.1.csv"),
                              na.strings = "")
distribution_data <- read.csv(file.path(cef_dir, "bll", "bll_2025_distributions_CEF_v17.1.csv"),
                              na.strings = "")

age_catch <- read.csv(file.path(cef_dir, "pok", "pok_2022_catches_CEF_v17.1.csv"),
                      na.strings = "")
age_dist  <- read.csv(file.path(cef_dir, "pok", "pok_2022_distributions_CEF_v17.1.csv"),
                      na.strings = "")
```

`derive_fields()` is what turns raw CEF into strata-ready data: it parses
`metier4` / `metier5` / `metier6` and `target` / `mesh` out of
`fleetValue`, and the ICES area levels (subarea, division, subdivision) out
of `areaValue`, plus `Stratum` - the same columns every plot function below
reads on `y` / `x` / `fill` / `facet`, alongside the native
`vesselFlagCountry` and `seasonValue`. The distributions need nothing of
the kind.

```{r derive}
catch_data <- derive_fields(x = catch_data)
age_catch  <- derive_fields(x = age_catch)

c(brill_catch = nrow(catch_data), brill_lengths = nrow(distribution_data),
  saithe_catch = nrow(age_catch), saithe_ages = nrow(age_dist))
table(distribution_data$distributionType)   # lengths only
table(age_dist$distributionType)            # ages only
```

Everything below reads `catch_data` / `distribution_data` (brill) except
the *Age coverage* and *Age distribution* sections, which read `age_catch` /
`age_dist` (saithe) instead - the brill file has no ages, and the saithe file
no lengths.

# The tables

`build_coverage_strata()` gives one row per stratum, at whatever aggregation
`dims` names, with no plotting involved. The columns follow the CAR / CAS
output tables - `total` is the discards D, `weightingTotal` the landings L
that carry a discard estimate, `rate` is `total / weightingTotal` (D/L),
`numTrips` the trips - in tonnes. `discardRate` is the same discards said the
other way, as a share of landings plus discards: `total / (weightingTotal +
total)` (D/(L+D)). Nothing in it judges the sampling: no status, no decision;
thresholds are a plotting choice.

```{r tab-disc}
cov_mc <- build_coverage_strata(catch = catch_data, dims = c("metier4", "vesselFlagCountry"))
head(cov_mc[order(-cov_mc$landings), ], 10)
```

The aggregation is yours - coarser:

```{r tab-coarse}
build_coverage_strata(catch = catch_data, dims = "metier4")
```

or finer:

```{r tab-fine}
cov_fine <- build_coverage_strata(catch = catch_data,
                                  dims = c("fleetValue", "areaValue", "seasonValue", "vesselFlagCountry"))
nrow(cov_fine)   # strata at fleetValue x areaValue x seasonValue x vesselFlagCountry
```

`dims` left out entirely pools nothing at all: `fleetValue`, `areaValue`,
`vesselFlagCountry` and `seasonValue`, whichever of those the catch actually carries - as
fine as the one above, just in that column order. It is the default
precisely so nothing is pooled away by accident - naming `dims` yourself is
how you ask for anything coarser.

```{r tab-finest}
cov_finest <- build_coverage_strata(catch = catch_data)
nrow(cov_finest)
identical(cov_finest, build_coverage_strata(catch = catch_data,
                                            dims = c("fleetValue", "areaValue", "vesselFlagCountry", "seasonValue")))
```

Every figure below takes the table as readily as the raw catch:
`plot_coverage_heat(catch = cov_mc, y = "metier4", x = "vesselFlagCountry")` draws the
same figure as `plot_coverage_heat(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", x =
"vesselFlagCountry")`. A
table built *finer* than the plotted columns is pooled to them - weights add
up, coverage and rate are re-derived from the summed weights, never
averaged.

# Discard coverage

`plot_coverage_heat()`, `_bubble()`, `_bar()` and `_map()`. Each takes raw
catch (or the table above) and, given raw catch, builds the table itself. `y`
is required. Heat and bubble put the second category on `x`; bars put it on
`fill`. `min_cov` and `min_trip` colour the heat and bubble status - a bar
chart ignores them (passing them is an error); `min_fish` is length/age
only, an error on a discard plot (no fish are measured for a discard
estimate). The status is worked out here from the thresholds, not stored in
the table. The status legend always lists
every *reachable* category - a stratum with no landed or caught weight at all
draws no cell (nothing to judge), so "no landings" is not one of them.

**Title, caption, and a boxed "Thresholds" guide.** There is no subtitle: the
caption's first line says what a stratum is - the columns you plot, grouped
over everything else ("grouping = metier4 x vesselFlagCountry, grouped over
... season"); put `seasonValue` on `facet` and it stops being grouped over. The rest
of the caption gives the formula behind the mark (a tile's value, a bubble's
size, the bar staircase) - never something a legend already shows (a
bubble's size scale, for instance, is never repeated in words). On the
heatmap and bubble grid the active thresholds move out of the caption
entirely, into their own bordered box bottom right, under the in-panel
status legend - a detail section of it, each threshold a formula, plus the
labelling rule.

## Bars: sampled against not-sampled weight

```{r disc-bar, fig.alt = "Sampled versus unsampled landed weight per metier"}
plot_coverage_bar(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", facet = "metier4")
```

## Heatmap: status per metier, country and season

```{r disc-heat-1, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "Coverage heatmap, metier by country, one panel per season"}
plot_coverage_heat(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", min_cov = 50, min_trip = 2)
```

The same with a trip threshold switched on:

```{r disc-heat-2, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "The same heatmap with a minimum of two trips"}
plot_coverage_heat(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", x = "vesselFlagCountry",
                   facet = "seasonValue", min_cov = 50, min_trip = 2)
```

## Bubbles: the weighted status grid

```{r disc-bubble, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Coverage bubble grid, bubble area proportional to landed weight"}
plot_coverage_bubble(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4",min_cov = 50, min_trip = 2)
```

Same grid as the heatmap, but a tiny un-sampled stratum now reads as a tiny
bubble - you can tell "small problem" from "the bulk of the fishery is
blind".

## Map: one pie per FAO area

One sampled / not-sampled pie per ICES area, radius = landings. `area` is the
level the pies are drawn at (`areaValue`, `ICESDivision`, `ICESSubArea`).
`group` puts a labelled box of pies per area, one pie per level.

```{r disc-map, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Coverage map, one sampled / not-sampled pie per area"}
plot_coverage_map(catch = catch_data, area = "ICESDivision", group = "metier4")
```

```{r disc-map-season, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Coverage map with one box of pies per area, split by season"}
plot_coverage_map(catch = catch_data, area = "ICESSubArea", group = "seasonValue")
```

```{r disc-map-country, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Coverage map with one box of pies per area, split by country"}
plot_coverage_map(catch = catch_data, group = "vesselFlagCountry")
```

# Length coverage

Pass `distributions` and `what = "length"`; `catchCategory` is `"Lan"`
throughout (see the top of the page for why). The table has one row per
stratum **and catch part**: the weight of the part, the share of it with a
distribution linked, and the measurements behind them.

```{r len-tab}
cov_len <- build_coverage_strata(catch = catch_data,
                                 dims = c("metier4", "vesselFlagCountry"),
                                 distributions = distribution_data,
                                 what = "length",
                                 catchCategory = "Lan")
head(cov_len[order(-cov_len$total), ], 10)
```

## Bars

Distributions attach to catch by `domainBiology`, so filtering the catch
alone is enough to narrow a figure (`metier4` is a catch-table column, not
one of the distributions).

```{r len-bar, fig.height = 9, fig.alt = "Length-sampled versus unsampled landed weight per metier, filled by country"}
plot_coverage_bar(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", fill = "vesselFlagCountry",
                  what = "length", catchCategory = "Lan",
                  distributions = distribution_data)
```

## Heatmap

At the finest fleet level - `fleetValue` - there are dozens of rows, so this
one is drawn without a `facet`; every facet repeats them.

```{r len-heat, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 10, fig.alt = "Length-sampling coverage of the landings by fleet and country"}
plot_coverage_heat(catch = catch_data, y = "fleetValue", x = "vesselFlagCountry",
                   what = "length", catchCategory = "Lan",
                   distributions = distribution_data,
                   min_cov = 70, min_fish = 100, min_trip = NULL)
```

## Bubbles

```{r len-bubble, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Length-sampling coverage of the landings, bubble grid"}
plot_coverage_bubble(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", x = "vesselFlagCountry",
                     what = "length", catchCategory = "Lan",
                     distributions = distribution_data,
                     min_cov = 50, min_fish = 100, min_trip = NULL)
```

## Map

The same pies as for the discards - radius = landed weight, coloured slice =
the share of it linked to a length distribution:

```{r len-map, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Length-sampling coverage map, one sampled / not-sampled pie per ICES division"}
plot_coverage_map(catch = catch_data, distributions = distribution_data,
                  what = "length", catchCategory = "Lan", area = "ICESDivision")
```

`group` puts a box of pies on each area, one pie per level - here one per
season:

```{r len-map-season, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Length-sampling coverage map with one box of pies per division, split by season"}
plot_coverage_map(catch = catch_data, distributions = distribution_data,
                  what = "length", catchCategory = "Lan",
                  area = "ICESDivision", group = "seasonValue")
```

```{r age-tab}
cov_age <- build_coverage_strata(catch = age_catch, dims = c("metier4", "vesselFlagCountry"),
                                 distributions = age_dist, what = "age", catchCategory = "Lan")
head(cov_age[order(-cov_age$total), ], 10)
```

## Bars

```{r age-bar, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Age-sampled versus unsampled landed weight per metier"}
plot_coverage_bar(catch = age_catch, y = "metier4",
                  what = "age", catchCategory = "Lan", distributions = age_dist)
```

## Heatmap

```{r age-heat, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Age-sampling coverage of the landings, metier by country"}
plot_coverage_heat(catch = age_catch, y = "metier4", x = "vesselFlagCountry",
                   what = "age", catchCategory = "Lan", distributions = age_dist,
                   min_cov = 50, min_fish = 100, min_trip = NULL)
```

## Bubbles

```{r age-bubble, fig.width = 8.5, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Age-sampling coverage of the landings, bubble grid"}
plot_coverage_bubble(catch = age_catch, y = "metier4", x = "vesselFlagCountry",
                     what = "age", catchCategory = "Lan", distributions = age_dist,
                     min_cov = 50, min_fish = 100, min_trip = NULL)
```

## Map

```{r age-map, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Age-sampling coverage map, one sampled / not-sampled pie per ICES division"}
plot_coverage_map(catch = age_catch, distributions = age_dist,
                  what = "age", catchCategory = "Lan", area = "ICESDivision")
```

```{r age-map-country, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "Age-sampling coverage map with one box of pies per division, split by country"}
plot_coverage_map(catch = age_catch, distributions = age_dist,
                  what = "age", catchCategory = "Lan",
                  area = "ICESDivision", group = "vesselFlagCountry")
```

# Discard rate

`plot_DR()` auto-builds the table from raw catch (or takes it). A
point is always an individual, un-pooled stratum: from raw catch the table is
built at the finest columns the catch carries, together with whatever you
plot (`x`, `colour`, `shape`, `facet`) - so several points can share one `x`
level, never merged into it. A stratum with no discard estimate has no rate
and gets no point; point size is the landings.

`rate` chooses the y variable and the word the title and axis use - both are
columns of the table. The y axis names the formula too, right next to the
word, so a reader never has to look the definition up:

* `"ratio"` (default, the discard ratio): `rate` = discards / landings(w/
  est.). Can exceed 100%, so the axis is pseudo-log. Axis: "Discard ratio (D/L)".
* `"rate"` (the discard rate): `discardRate` = discards / catch(w/ est.).
  Bounded 0-100%, so the axis is an ordinary one. Axis: "Discard rate (D/(L+D))".

A thin grey line behind the points (no diamond) marks each `x` level's mean,
weighted by landings - for the ratio, `build_coverage_strata(catch =
catch_data, dims = "metier4")`'s rate directly.

```{r dr, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Discard rate per metier and country, one point per stratum, a line for the weighted mean of each metier"}
plot_DR(catch = catch_data,x = "metier4",colour = "vesselFlagCountry",jitter = TRUE, rate = "rate",reference = 0.5)
```

Faceted by area, the strata are unaffected (they were already the finest the
catch carries) - only the panels change:

```{r dr-facet, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "Discard rate per stratum, by metier, coloured by country, one panel per area"}
plot_DR(catch = catch_data,
       x = "metier4",
       colour = "vesselFlagCountry",
       facet = "areaValue",
       jitter = TRUE)
```

`reference` draws a dashed line at a rate and names the strata above it, so
the ones to look at are on the figure - a fraction on the scale of the `rate`
you chose (`0.3` is 30%). Each label is the stratum's identity in full - bare
values, only the finest column of each family (a coarser alias already
determined by a finer one you also plotted, `metier4` alongside `fleetValue`
say, is left out), joined by `|`: a point is an individual raw stratum now,
so `MIS|Denmark` alone could still be several areas or seasons - the label
always says which.

```{r dr-ref, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Discard rate per metier and country, a dashed reference line at 30%, the strata above it labelled"}
plot_DR(catch = catch_data, x = "metier4", colour = "vesselFlagCountry",
       rate = "rate", reference = 0.3)
```

The labelled strata are the rows of the finest-resolution table above the
line:

```{r dr-ref-tab}
above <- build_coverage_strata(catch = catch_data,
                               dims = c("fleetValue", "areaValue", "vesselFlagCountry",
                                        "seasonValue", "metier4"))
above <- above[!is.na(above$discardRate) & above$discardRate > 0.3, ]
above[order(-above$discardRate),
      c("metier4", "vesselFlagCountry", "fleetValue", "areaValue", "seasonValue",
        "total", "weightingTotal", "rate", "discardRate")]
```

# Discard-rate clusters

A different question from the discard rate itself: which strata *share* a
rate, and which of `metier4`, `mesh`, `vesselFlagCountry`, `seasonValue`
and `areaValue` actually predicts that? Most of those are categorical, so an ordinary PCA
does not apply - `build_discard_clusters()` uses MCA (Multiple Correspondence
Analysis) instead, the categorical equivalent, to place every stratum on a
map from how its categories co-occur. Clustering itself runs on the discard
rate alone (`k` groups, k-means), not on the MCA coordinates, so a cluster
always means "similar discard rate" - the map is only where those clusters
are then shown.

```{r clusters}
dc <- build_discard_clusters(catch_data,
                             dims = c("metier4", "mesh", "vesselFlagCountry", "seasonValue",
                                      "areaValue"))
dc$importance
```

On the map, an ellipse per cluster shows whether it occupies its own part of
variable space or is scattered through it - and the axes rarely capture more
than a fifth of the total structure, so read it as a sketch, not the full
picture:

```{r clusters-map, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Every stratum on the MCA map of metier4, mesh, vesselFlagCountry, seasonValue and areaValue, coloured by its discard-rate cluster, with an ellipse per cluster"}
plot_discard_clusters(dc)
```

Which variable actually drives the clustering - Cramer's V of each against
the cluster, 0 unrelated, 1 fully determining it:

```{r clusters-importance, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Cramer's V of metier4, mesh, vesselFlagCountry, seasonValue and areaValue against the discard-rate cluster, sorted strongest first"}
plot_cluster_variables(dc)
```

# Length distribution

`plot_NaLoA()` is a histogram (`variableType` is always `Number`);
`plot_MWaLoA()` is a line, always - Numbers and Mean Weight at Length or
Age. Both take a prepared table **or** raw catch plus `distributions` - then
the link and the summary run inside, with `catchCategory` choosing the part.
Numbers are in thousands (N3), length in cm. The caption's first line names
the stratum a bar or a line pools: the sampled strata that share the plotted
columns (`fill` or `colour`, and `facet`); everything else is grouped into
it. The rest gives the arithmetic: bars are NaL/NaA (numbers at length/age)
summed over those strata, a line is MWaL/MWaA (mean weight) weighted by
numbers measured, with a ribbon for the spread across them. Distributions
reach the catch through `domainBiology` **and the country**: two countries
can use the same domain name, each with its own distributions, and a
country's strata get only its own.

## Numbers at length

```{r num-len, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Numbers at length of the landings, stacked by country, one panel per metier"}
plot_NaLoA(data = catch_data, distributions = distribution_data, distributionType = "LengthTotal", catchCategory = "Lan", fill = "metier4", stacked = TRUE)
```

## Mean weight at length

```{r mw-len, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Mean weight at length of the landings, one line per country, one panel per season"}
plot_MWaLoA(data = catch_data, distributions = distribution_data, distributionType = "LengthTotal", colour = "metier4", show_samples = TRUE)
```

### The fish behind each point

A mean weight that rests on a few fish is uncertain however smooth the line
looks. `show_samples = TRUE` draws, behind the lines, semi-transparent bars of
the fish measured at each length, read on the axis on the right. They are
stacked by `colour`, so each country's fish at a length are its own segment,
and they share one scale across the panels:

```{r mw-len-n, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Mean weight at length of the landings with bars of the fish measured behind the lines, one panel per season"}
plot_MWaLoA(data = catch_data, distributions = distribution_data,
           distributionType = "LengthTotal",
           catchCategory = "Lan", colour = "vesselFlagCountry",
           facet = "seasonValue", show_samples = TRUE)
```

The distributions record `numMeasurements` once for a whole distribution, not
per length, so the fish at a length are that count shared out over the
distribution's lengths in proportion to its numbers - exact for a length
sample raised by one factor, an estimate otherwise. The caption says so, and
says when a point has no bar because its distributions report no count (a
sample size that is unknown, not zero).

`n_fish` is a column of the summary the plot is built from, so the counts can
be read as numbers too - the thin ends of the curve are where they are small:

```{r mw-len-n-tab}
linked <- link_dist_to_strata(catches = catch_data, dist = distribution_data,
                              dims = c("catchCategory", "vesselFlagCountry"),
                              catch_category = "Lan", type = "LengthTotal")
mw_len <- length_meanweight(linked = linked, group_vars = "vesselFlagCountry")
head(mw_len[order(mw_len$n_fish), c(".class", "vesselFlagCountry", "mean_weight", "n_strata", "n_fish")], 8)
```

# Thresholds

`min_cov` is always part of the classification. `min_trip` (discard, length,
age) and `min_fish` (length, age only) are each independently **optional**:
`NULL` drops that question from the classification and the legend entirely,
a number turns it on. On the plot functions both default to `NULL`, so a
call with no `min_trip` at all is coverage-only already.

`min_trip = 0` is *not* the same as `NULL`: it is still an active (if lenient)
threshold, and a stratum with no reported trip count fails an active trips
test no matter how low it is set - unknown is never treated as adequate.

`cat_lookup()` shows exactly which categories are reachable for a given
combination. It is a lower-level function than the plots and keeps its own
default of `min_trips = 2` (active) when called directly:

```{r thr-lookup}
cat_lookup(threshold = 50, what = "discard", min_trips = NULL)$cat_key   # coverage only
cat_lookup(threshold = 50, what = "discard")$cat_key                     # + trips (its own default)
cat_lookup(threshold = 50, what = "length", min_meas = 25)$cat_key       # + measurements too
```

The colour is a straight count of how many *active* targets a stratum missed
- yellow for one, orange for two, dark orange for three (only reachable with
trips **and** measurements both on) - but each specific combination is still
its own category and its own label. **Red** stays reserved for "no discard
estimate" / "no distribution linked at all" on a stratum that *has* weight:
never a threshold miss, and never a stratum with no weight at all (that draws
no cell to begin with).

```{r thr-heat-cov, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Coverage heatmap, coverage alone"}
plot_coverage_heat(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", x = "vesselFlagCountry", min_trip = NULL)
```

```{r thr-heat-trip, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Coverage heatmap with trips added"}
plot_coverage_heat(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", x = "vesselFlagCountry")
```

```{r thr-heat-len, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Length coverage heatmap, coverage and measurements"}
plot_coverage_heat(catch = catch_data, y = "metier4", x = "vesselFlagCountry",
                   what = "length", catchCategory = "Lan",
                   distributions = distribution_data,
                   min_trip = NULL, min_fish = 25)
```

Setting the thresholds absurdly high must **not** turn every stratum red: it
crowds them into the worst-active warning shade instead. Red only ever comes
from "no estimate / no distribution", never from a threshold comparison:

```{r thr-extreme}
extreme <- classify_strata(s = build_strata(catch_data = catch_data, dims = c("metier4", "vesselFlagCountry")),
                           threshold = 1500, min_trips = 1000)
table(extreme$cat_key)
# red ("no_dist") only where there really is no discard estimate
all(!extreme$has_disc_data[extreme$cat_key == "no_dist"])
```

# Age distribution (saithe)

Numbers, mean weight and the plus group at age - the same functions as the
length distributions above, with `distributionType = "Age"`, on the saithe
file (`age_catch` / `age_dist`). Landings throughout.

## Numbers and mean weight at age

```{r age-num, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Numbers at age of the landings, stacked by country"}
plot_NaLoA(data = age_catch, distributions = age_dist, distributionType = "Age",
          catchCategory = "Lan", fill = "vesselFlagCountry",
          stacked = TRUE)
```

```{r age-num-facet, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "Numbers at age of the landings, one panel per season"}
plot_NaLoA(data = age_catch, distributions = age_dist, distributionType = "Age",
          catchCategory = "Lan", fill = "metier4",
          facet = "seasonValue", stacked = TRUE)
```

```{r age-mw, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Mean weight at age of the landings, one line per country"}
plot_MWaLoA(data = age_catch, distributions = age_dist, distributionType = "Age",
           catchCategory = "Lan", colour = "vesselFlagCountry", facet = "seasonValue")
```

### The plus group

The oldest ages are a handful of fish each, so the right-hand end of a
mean-weight curve is ragged. `plus_group = 7` pools every age from 7 upward
into one class - labelled `7+` on the axis and in the caption - to show what
a plus group does to the curve. Inside each distribution the numbers of
those ages are added and their mean weights averaged, weighted by those
numbers; the pooled class is then averaged over strata like any other point,
so the ribbon is still a spread across strata, not across ages. It is for
ages only (a hard error on lengths), and needs raw catch with `distributions`
(a summary that has already been averaged cannot be pooled again).

```{r age-mw-plus, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Mean weight at age of the landings with ages 7 and older pooled into 7+, one line per country"}
plot_MWaLoA(data = age_catch, distributions = age_dist, distributionType = "Age",
           catchCategory = "Lan", colour = "vesselFlagCountry",
           plus_group = 7)
```

The start is yours to move. One line for all countries, without and with the
plus group from 5, 10 and 15:

```{r age-mw-plus-sweep, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Mean weight at age of the landings without a plus group and with plus groups from 5, 10 and 15"}
print(plot_MWaLoA(data = age_catch, distributions = age_dist, distributionType = "Age",
                  catchCategory = "Lan"))
for (start in c(5, 10, 15)) {
  print(plot_MWaLoA(data = age_catch, distributions = age_dist, distributionType = "Age",
                    catchCategory = "Lan",
                    plus_group = start))
}
```

### The fish behind each point

`show_samples = TRUE` puts the fish measured at each age behind the lines, on
the axis on the right, so a mean weight that rests on a few fish shows. Each
age's count is the distribution's `numMeasurements` shared out over its ages
in proportion to its numbers - an estimate for ages, which are read off an
age-length key - summed over the pooled strata and stacked by `colour`. Several
countries in this saithe file report `numMeasurements` 0 for their age
distributions: their points have mean weights and numbers but no bar - an
unknown sample size, not zero - and the caption says so.

```{r age-mw-n, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Mean weight at age of the landings with bars of the fish measured behind the lines, one line per country"}
plot_MWaLoA(data = age_catch, distributions = age_dist, distributionType = "Age",
           catchCategory = "Lan", colour = "vesselFlagCountry", facet = "metier4",
           show_samples = TRUE,
           plus_group = 7)
```

Together, for one line (no `colour`): the plus group turns the thin tail of
old ages, each on a few fish, into one point with many.

```{r age-mw-plus-n, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Mean weight at age of the landings with a plus group from 10 and bars of the fish measured"}
plot_MWaLoA(data = age_catch, distributions = age_dist, distributionType = "Age",
           catchCategory = "Lan", show_samples = TRUE,
           plus_group = 7)
```
